propositions.text: Mr. Habibi is a 64-year-old Iranian citizen and former police officer who sought refugee protection in Canada with his wife in 2012.
propositions.quote: Mr. Habibi is a 64 year old citizen of Iran who spent approximately 28 years as a police officer in Iran.

propositions.text: Their refugee claims were denied by the RPD in a January 22, 2015 decision.
propositions.quote: Their claims were denied, however, by the Refugee Protection Division [RPD] of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada in a decision dated January 22, 2015.

propositions.text: They seek judicial review of the RPD decision under subsection 72(1) of IRPA, asking for the decision to be set aside and claims re-determined by a new RPD panel.
propositions.quote: They now seek judicial review of the RPD’s decision pursuant to subsection 72(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 [IRPA], asking the Court to set aside the decision and order that their claims be re-determined by a new panel of the RPD.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Habibi and wife sought refugee protection in 2012, were denied by RPD in 2015, and now seek judicial review to set aside that decision.

propositions.text: Mr. Habibi was raised Muslim but had distant Christian ancestry and a Christian best friend in high school.
propositions.quote: Mr. Habibi was raised as a Muslim, although his family did have distant Christian ancestry. During high school, he became interested in Christianity and had a best friend who was an Armenian Christian.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Mr. Habibi's Muslim upbringing with distant Christian ancestry and a Christian friend in high school.

propositions.text: Mr. Habibi served mandatory military service from 1971-1973, then worked as a criminal investigation officer in Tabriz police.
propositions.quote: In May 1971, Mr. Habibi began his mandatory two years of military service with the Iranian infantry; after that service ended in 1973 he started working as a criminal investigation officer in the District 8 Police Station in Tabriz, a large city in northern Iran.

propositions.text: From 1985-1987, he studied criminology at Tehran Municipal Police University and graduated with a diploma.
propositions.quote: From November 1985 until November 1987, he spent two years at Tehran Municipal Police University; he graduated with a Diploma in Criminology.

propositions.text: He returned to Tabriz police in 1987, later trained recruits from 1998 until retirement in 2002, reaching Lieutenant Colonel rank.
propositions.quote: In November 1987, he returned to Tabriz to work for the criminal investigation department of the police force and, subsequently, from March 1998 until 2002 when he retired, Mr. Habibi trained new recruits for that department. By the time of his retirement, he had obtained the rank of Lieutenant Colonel in the Disciplinary Forces of the Islamic Republic of Iran.

propositions.text: He witnessed regime suppression of minorities, became disenchanted with Islam, but stayed silent fearing job loss, imprisonment, or torture.
propositions.quote: After his return to Tabriz in 1987, Mr. Habibi says he witnessed the revolutionary regime’s suppression of ethnic and religious minorities and became disenchanted with Islam, yet stayed silent because he feared not only loss of his job, but also imprisonment and torture if he spoke out.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes Mr. Habibi's military and police career, education, disenchantment with Islam, and fear of speaking out.

propositions.text: After retirement, Mr. Habibi opened a bookstore in Karaj in 2003 and befriended a young Christian couple.
propositions.quote: After his retirement, Mr. Habibi moved to Karaj, Iran, and opened a bookstore there in September 2003. Among his customers was a young Christian couple with whom Mr. Habibi developed a friendship.

propositions.text: He and his wife expressed interest in Christianity and began attending underground Christian services in 2004.
propositions.quote: After inviting the couple to his home, Mr. Habibi and his wife expressed their interest in Christianity and this, in turn, led to an invitation to attend the couple’s underground Christian services. In May 2004, Mr. Habibi started attending the underground services; his wife attended only a few times though because of concern for her safety.

propositions.text: By April 2006, Mr. Habibi, his wife, and youngest son had converted to Christianity.
propositions.quote: By April 2006, Mr. Habibi had converted to Christianity as had his wife and their youngest son, who was then 20 years old.

propositions.text: He distributed Christian Bibles and fliers through his bookstore to underground church members' referrals.
propositions.quote: Prior to and after his conversion, Mr. Habibi distributed Christian Bibles and fliers through his bookstore to individuals referred to him by underground church members.

paragraphs.summary: The court recounts Mr. Habibi's post-retirement bookstore, Christian conversion, and distribution of Christian materials.

propositions.text: In March 2012, Mr. Habibi's underground church was raided; parishioners arrested and he was warned authorities sought him.
propositions.quote: On March 26, 2012, Mr. Habibi’s underground church was raided by intelligence officers and some of his fellow parishioners arrested. The next day, while on a business trip in Tehran, Mr. Habibi learned of the raid and, after he was warned that the authorities were looking for him...

propositions.text: He fled to Canada on March 30, 2012, using a visitor visa; his bookstore and home were searched and an arrest warrant issued for him.
propositions.quote: Mr. Habibi remained in Tehran until March 30, 2012, when he fled to Canada utilizing a visitor’s visa he had previously obtained. Shortly after Mr. Habibi fled to Canada, his bookstore and house were searched by the intelligence authorities who brought an arrest warrant for him...

propositions.text: Ms. Khoshadel was detained twice and released without arrest after denying conversion to Christianity.
propositions.quote: ...informing Ms. Khoshadel he was an infidel and evangelizing others to become Christians and detaining her for questioning; she denied having converted to Christianity and was released. Two days later, Ms. Khoshadel was again detained and questioned but was again released without being arrested.

propositions.text: Their youngest son went into hiding and fled to Germany, where he was granted refugee protection.
propositions.quote: ...their youngest son went into hiding and subsequently fled to Germany where he was eventually granted refugee protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court details the 2012 raid, Mr. Habibi's flight to Canada, his wife's detentions, and their son's flight to Germany.

propositions.text: Ms. Khoshadel obtained a visa to Canada in October 2012 and arrived November 3, 2012, then they claimed refugee protection together.
propositions.quote: Ms. Khoshadel secured a visa to travel to Canada in October 2012... After she arrived in Canada on November 3, 2012, Ms. Khoshadel and her husband [together, the Applicants] made a claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: The RPD hearing started May 12, 2013, was adjourned twice for Minister's intervention due to Mr. Habibi's police involvement, then proceeded September 9, 2014.
propositions.quote: The RPD hearing commenced on May 12, 2013, but was adjourned twice in order to invite the Minister’s intervention due to Mr. Habibi’s involvement with the Iranian national police force. The hearing proceeded on September 9, 2014...

propositions.text: On March 18, 2015, the RPD found Mr. Habibi excluded from refugee protection under Article 1F(a) and that the Applicants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.
propositions.quote: ...in a decision dated March 18, 2015, the RPD found that because Mr. Habibi is a person referred to in Article 1F (a) of the Convention... he is excluded from refugee protection by virtue of section 98 of the IRPA. The RPD also determined that the Applicants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Khoshadel joined Mr. Habibi in Canada, they claimed refugee protection, and the RPD excluded Mr. Habibi under Article 1F(a).

propositions.text: The RPD acknowledged Mr. Habibi’s counsel’s submissions on the need for evidence of personal, significant, knowing participation in crimes for exclusion.
propositions.quote: In its decision, the RPD acknowledged the submissions of Mr. Habibi’s counsel that, for him to be excluded from refugee protection, there had to be evidence of him having a personal, significant, and knowing participation in crimes or crimes against humanity; and that he should not be excluded because there was no evidence he personally made a voluntary, knowing and significant contribution to the crimes or criminal purposes of the Iranian regime.

propositions.text: The RPD adopted the Minister’s conclusion that Mr. Habibi’s retirement after 28 years did not show efforts to distance himself from the offending organization.
propositions.quote: ...the RPD adopted as its own the Minister’s conclusion that Mr. Habibi’s retirement after 28 years’ service as a police officer did not “connote an individual who has been making long standing efforts to divorce himself from an offending organization at the earliest opportunity.”

paragraphs.summary: The RPD recognized counsel’s argument on exclusion requiring personal participation and adopted the Minister’s view on Mr. Habibi’s retirement.

propositions.text: The RPD noted Mr. Habibi’s claim his department handled only minor crimes, but found he likely knew and directed police cooperation with other agencies.
propositions.quote: The RPD noted Mr. Habibi’s insistence that his department looked after only domestic issues and minor crimes and the police looked after public security. Nonetheless, the RPD found that: [25] … even if the PC’s department was not involved in some of the actions of certain units such as enforcing musical choices or “appropriate” public behaviour, it would most certainly be aware of other actions and likely supported their enforcement. As a Colonel in the national police and a career police officer, the panel finds that, more likely than not, he, not only would have been aware of the police’s co-operation with and support for other agencies such as the Komiteh, but also have been involved in providing direction to the actions of police when working with other agencies.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Mr. Habibi likely aware of and directing police cooperation with other enforcement agencies despite his claims.

propositions.text: Mr. Habibi denied transferring prisoners to agencies committing crimes, but the RPD accepted Minister’s evidence police worked closely with such agencies.
propositions.quote: Although Mr. Habibi testified that he and his department had never transferred a prisoner to another security or enforcement agency which had committed crimes and crimes against humanity, such as the Pasdaran, Komiteh, Basij or Ministry of Intelligence and Security, the RPD accepted the Minister’s documentary evidence in this regard, noting that such evidence “indicates that the police worked closely” with such agencies.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD accepted Minister’s evidence police cooperated with agencies committing crimes, despite Mr. Habibi’s denial.

propositions.text: No specific evidence showed Mr. Habibi’s direct involvement in crimes against humanity.
propositions.quote: The RPD acknowledged there is no specific evidence of Mr. Habibi’s direct involvement in any acts by agents of the Iranian regime which were crimes against humanity.

propositions.text: Given his rank and service, it is reasonable to conclude Mr. Habibi was aware of and involved directly or indirectly in crimes against humanity.
propositions.quote: [28] … given the PC’s voluntary service of 28 years and his senior rank in the Iranian police force, who actively supported other security/enforcement agencies, it is reasonable to conclude that he was well aware, not only of the activities of the other agencies, but also of the police’s involvement with and support of their actions against the Iranian people. Given his profile, it is also reasonable to conclude that he would have been involved directly or indirectly through direction to others in acts which have been determined by international law to be “crimes against humanity”.

propositions.text: The Minister met the burden to show serious reasons to consider Mr. Habibi committed a crime under Article 1F(a).
propositions.quote: The RPD thus concluded that the Minister had met the burden of proof to show that “there are serious reasons for considering” that Mr. Habibi has “committed a crime” as contemplated by Article 1F (a) of the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found no direct evidence of crimes but reasonably concluded Mr. Habibi was aware and involved, meeting burden for exclusion under Article 1F(a).

propositions.text: The RPD found Mr. Habibi not credible due to implausibility of ignorance, service inconsistencies, and contradictions about wife’s detentions.
propositions.quote: After concluding that Mr. Habibi had committed a crime as contemplated by Article 1F (a), the RPD next assessed his credibility. It found he was not a credible witness, stating that it was implausible that he was not aware of the actions of other enforcement agencies. In the RPD’s view, Mr. Habibi was not credible because: (a) there was no evidence of a break in his service despite his claim of being suspended and in hiding for three months following the 1979 revolution; (b) there were inconsistencies between the number of witnesses who provided evidence to the authorities about his Christian actions and how many were required to prove anything against him; and (c) Mr. Habibi attributed his wife’s detentions and releases to a lack of documentation against her and assistance from his friends, yet at the same time indicated that these friends would not be able to help him and acknowledged that the authorities might detain his wife to get at him.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD found Mr. Habibi not credible due to implausible ignorance, service inconsistencies, and contradictory explanations about wife’s detentions.

propositions.text: The RPD questioned why Applicants needed Bible study in Toronto if practicing Christians in Iran and noted Ms. Khoshadel was not arrested despite accusations.
propositions.quote: In assessing the Applicants’ fear of persecution, the RPD questioned why they were required to go to Bible study sessions in Toronto if they had been practicing Christians in Iran. In addition, the RPD noted that although Ms. Khoshadel was accused of converting to Christianity, she was not arrested...

propositions.text: Due to credibility concerns, the RPD found insufficient evidence that Applicants left Iran due to authorities searching for them for conversion or that they were underground church members.
propositions.quote: Accordingly, in view of its credibility concerns, the RPD concluded there was insufficient reliable or trustworthy evidence to show: that the Applicants left Iran because the authorities are searching for them due to their conversion to Christianity; that they were ever members of an underground church in Iran...

propositions.text: The RPD found it more likely Applicants joined a Canadian church to support their refugee claim, not due to faith.
propositions.quote: ...or that they were motivated to join a Christian church in Canada because of their faith, since it was more likely than not they joined to establish a basis for their claim for refugee protection.

propositions.text: The RPD determined Applicants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection, and Mr. Habibi is excluded under Article 1F(a).
propositions.quote: The RPD thus determined that neither of the Applicants is a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, and that Mr. Habibi was excluded from refugee protection as contemplated by Article 1F (a) of the Convention.

paragraphs.summary: The RPD doubted Applicants’ fear of persecution and found insufficient evidence of persecution or genuine faith, concluding they are not refugees and Mr. Habibi is excluded.

propositions.text: The Court identifies three issues: standard of review, proper test for complicity under Article 1F(a), and reasonableness of RPD’s credibility finding.
propositions.quote: While the parties raise various issues, only three need to be addressed by the Court, namely: 1. What is the Standard of Review? 2. Did the RPD adopt and apply the proper test for complicity in international crimes for purposes of Article 1F (a) of the Convention? and 3. Was it unreasonable for the RPD to find the Applicants’ fear of persecution not credible?

paragraphs.summary: The court states it will address three issues: standard of review, RPD’s test for complicity, and reasonableness of credibility finding.

propositions.text: The Court agrees with Applicants that the standard of review for RPD’s interpretation of Article 1F(a) is correctness, with no deference owed.
propositions.quote: I agree with the Applicants that the standard of review for the RPD’s interpretation of Article 1F (a) is correctness. Hence, its interpretation of the scope of Article 1F (a) is owed no deference by the Court.

paragraphs.summary: The court agrees the standard of review for RPD’s interpretation of Article 1F(a) is correctness, with no deference.

propositions.text: Febles FCA held correctness is the standard for RPD’s interpretation of Article 1F(b) to ensure uniform interpretation of international Convention provisions.
propositions.quote: In Hernandez Febles v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2012 FCA 324... the Federal Court of Appeal offered the following rationale for why the applicable standard for the RPD’s interpretation of Article 1F of the Convention is one of correctness: [24] … the normal presumption that reasonableness is the standard of review applicable to tribunals’ interpretation of their enabling statute does not apply in this case. Article 1F (b) is a provision of an international Convention that should be interpreted as uniformly as possible: see, for example, Jayasekara at para. 4. Correctness review is more likely than reasonableness review to achieve this goal, and is therefore the standard to be applied for determining whether the RPD erred in law by interpreting Article 1F (b) as precluding consideration of Mr Febles’ post-conviction rehabilitation and his present dangerousness. Further, the interpretation of Article 1F (b) does not give rise to any ambiguity.

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Febles FCA explaining correctness standard for RPD’s interpretation of Article 1F to ensure uniformity of international law.

propositions.text: The Supreme Court did not comment on or expressly uphold the Febles FCA determination on standard of review when overturning that decision.
propositions.quote: This determination was neither commented upon nor expressly upheld by the Supreme Court when it overturned the Court of Appeal’s decision in Febles v. Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 SCC 68, [2014] 3 SCR 431.

paragraphs.summary: The court notes the Supreme Court did not comment on or uphold the Febles FCA standard of review determination when overturning that decision.

propositions.text: The RPD’s findings on Applicants’ fear of persecution are reviewed on a reasonableness standard, requiring intelligible, transparent, justifiable decisions within acceptable outcomes.
propositions.quote: As for the other aspects of the RPD’s decision, notably as to the RPD’s finding that the Applicants’ fear of persecution was not credible, these are to be reviewed on the reasonableness standard. Accordingly, the Court should not interfere if the RPD’s decision is intelligible, transparent, and justifiable, and falls within a range of possible, acceptable outcomes defensible in respect of the facts and the law: Dunsmuir v New Brunswick, 2008 SCC 9 at para 47, [2008] 1 SCR 190.

propositions.text: Reasonableness review requires reasons allowing court to understand tribunal’s decision and determine if conclusion is acceptable: Newfoundland Nurses Union.
propositions.quote: Those criteria are met if “the reasons allow the reviewing court to understand why the tribunal made its decision and permit it to determine whether the conclusion is within the range of acceptable outcomes”: Newfoundland and Labrador Nurses’ Union v Newfoundland and Labrador (Treasury Board), 2011 SCC 62 at para 16, [2011] 3 SCR 708.

propositions.text: It is not the court’s role to reweigh evidence or substitute its own view of preferable outcome: Khosa SCC.
propositions.quote: It is not up to this Court to reweigh the evidence that was before the RPD, and it is not the function of this Court to substitute its own view of a preferable outcome: Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 59 and 61, [2009] 1 SCR 339.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness standard for reviewing RPD’s credibility findings, citing Dunsmuir, Newfoundland Nurses, and Khosa.

propositions.text: The RPD did not reference Ezokola test for complicity but this alone does not make its decision unreasonable.
propositions.quote: Although the RPD’s decision is devoid of any reference to the test and factors for complicity emanating from the Supreme Court’s decision in Ezokola v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 SCC 40, [2013] 2 SCR 678 [Ezokola], that fact alone does not make its decision unreasonable (see: Aazamyar v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2015 FC 99, at para 36, 249 ACWS (3d) 188).

propositions.text: The RPD acknowledged counsel’s submissions that exclusion requires evidence of voluntary, knowing, significant contribution to crimes or criminal purposes.
propositions.quote: The RPD did acknowledge the submissions of Mr. Habibi’s counsel that in order for Mr. Habibi to be excluded from refugee protection, there had to be evidence of him personally making a voluntary, knowing and significant contribution to crimes against humanity or the criminal purposes of the Iranian regime; at least to this extent, the RPD was somewhat mindful of the test for complicity.

propositions.text: Minister’s submissions directed the RPD to Ezokola and its six non-exhaustive factors for complicity.
propositions.quote: Furthermore, the Minister’s written submissions explicitly directed the RPD to Ezokola and, in particular, to the six non-exhaustive factors identified by the Supreme Court which serve as a guide to deciding whether an individual has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to a crime or criminal purpose of an organization with which the individual is associated.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD’s lack of Ezokola reference alone is not unreasonable; RPD acknowledged counsel’s submissions and Minister’s Ezokola guidance.

propositions.text: The RPD unreasonably applied the complicity test, relying on rejected 'guilt by association' rather than Ezokola’s refined test and factors.
propositions.quote: However, in this case, even if it might be said that the RPD understood the Ezokola test for complicity, it incorrectly and unreasonably applied the test. Its decision as a whole rests more upon a “guilt by association” approach to complicity, an approach which was explicitly rejected in Ezokola, than upon the refined test and factors for complicity emanating from Ezokola.

propositions.text: Therefore, the matter must be returned for re-determination by a different RPD panel member.
propositions.quote: Consequently, for the reasons that follow, the matter must be returned for re-determination by a different panel member of the RPD in accordance with these reasons.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD unreasonably applied complicity test relying on guilt by association and orders re-determination by a different panel.

propositions.text: Ezokola test requires serious reasons to consider voluntary, knowing, significant contribution to crime or criminal purpose of group.
propositions.quote: The test for complicity following Ezokola requires that there be “serious reasons for considering that …[an individual] voluntarily made a knowing and significant contribution to the crime or criminal purpose of the group alleged to have committed the crime” (para 29).

propositions.text: Ezokola’s three requirements: voluntary, significant, and knowing contribution to crime or criminal purpose.
propositions.quote: There are three requirements under the test: (1) a voluntary contribution to the crime or criminal purpose; (2) a significant contribution to the group’s crime or criminal purpose; and (3) a knowing contribution to the crime or criminal purpose (at paras 86-90).

propositions.text: Parties agree Mr. Habibi’s police service was voluntary; dispute is on significant and knowing contribution and police knowledge of crimes.
propositions.quote: Neither party suggests that Mr. Habibi joining and working for the national police force was anything other than voluntary; indeed, he served with that force for some 28 years. Rather, their arguments focus upon whether he made any significant and knowing contribution to any crimes against humanity or the criminal purposes of the Revolutionary regime, and whether the national police force was even privy to any such crimes or purposes.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains Ezokola’s complicity test and notes parties agree on voluntariness but dispute significant and knowing contribution and police knowledge.

propositions.text: Significant and knowing contribution depends on facts; Supreme Court's Ezokola factors guide assessment of complicity.
propositions.quote: Whether there is a significant and knowing contribution depends on the facts of each case. In applying the test, the Supreme Court offered the following guidance in Ezokola: [91] Whether there are serious reasons for considering that an individual has committed international crimes will depend on the facts of each case. Accordingly, to determine whether an individual’s conduct meets the actus reus and mens rea for complicity, several factors may be of assistance. The following…factors…should serve as a guide in assessing whether an individual has voluntarily made a significant and knowing contribution to a crime or criminal purpose: (i) the size and nature of the organization; (ii) the part of the organization with which the refugee claimant was most directly concerned; (iii) the refugee claimant’s duties and activities in the organization; (iv) the refugee claimant’s rank or position in the organization; (v) the length of time the claimant was in the organization, particularly after acquiring knowledge of the group’s crime or criminal purpose; and (vi) the method by which the claimant was recruited and the claimant’s opportunity to leave the organization. …

paragraphs.summary: The court states that significant and knowing contribution depends on facts, guided by Supreme Court's Ezokola factors for complicity.

propositions.text: Ezokola emphasizes contextual application of factors to determine voluntary, significant, knowing contribution to crime.
propositions.quote: The Supreme Court noted in Ezokola that application of these factors is highly contextual, with the ultimate purpose “to determine whether there was a voluntary, significant, and knowing contribution to a crime or criminal purpose” (at para 92).

paragraphs.summary: The court notes Ezokola's emphasis on contextual application of factors to assess voluntary, significant, knowing contribution to crime.

propositions.text: RPD referenced some Ezokola factors: Habibi's rank, recruitment, opportunity to leave, and his acknowledgment of human rights violations.
propositions.quote: For example, the RPD did note Mr. Habibi’s rank or position as a Lieutenant Colonel in the national police force, as well as the manner by which he joined that organization and his opportunity to leave it. The RPD also highlighted that Mr. Habibi acknowledged human rights violations under the regime and expressed his distaste for the government’s actions, yet he did not attempt to leave government service.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker referenced some Ezokola factors regarding Habibi's rank, recruitment, opportunity to leave, and acknowledgment of violations.

propositions.text: RPD's assessment of Habibi's complicity was generalized and unjustified; no specific evidence of direct involvement found.
propositions.quote: However, in the circumstances of this case, the RPD’s overall assessment of Mr. Habibi’s alleged complicity was at best generalized, and its conclusion that there are serious reasons for considering that Mr. Habibi has committed a crime as contemplated by Article 1F (a) of the Convention cannot be justified.

propositions.text: RPD failed to fully and transparently assess the six Ezokola factors, mostly concurring with Minister's conclusions.
propositions.quote: This being so, the RPD should have clearly set its mind to a full and transparent assessment and analysis of the relevancy and weight of the six factors noted above, rather than, for the most part, simply concurring with the Minister’s conclusions.

propositions.text: Failure to explicitly state test and factors is not fatal but indicates unreasonable consideration by RPD.
propositions.quote: The failure to explicitly set out the test and factors for complicity, while in itself not a fatal flaw in the RPD’s decision, strongly indicates that the RPD did not reasonably or properly consider the six factors and their respective relevance or weight in Mr. Habibi’s case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD's assessment generalized, unjustified, failed full analysis of Ezokola factors, and did not reasonably consider them.

propositions.text: RPD did not address size and nature of police force or district where Habibi worked.
propositions.quote: For example, nowhere in its reasons does the RPD address the size and nature of either the national police force as a whole or the District police station where Mr. Habibi worked.

propositions.text: Documentary evidence shows national police numbered about 50,000 in mid-1980s, engaged in usual urban police activities.
propositions.quote: The documentary evidence suggests that the national police force numbered some 50,000 members during the mid-1980s and engaged in “the usual urban police activities.”

propositions.text: Ezokola states size of organization helps determine likelihood of claimant's knowledge and participation; heterogeneous organizations weaken link.
propositions.quote: In Ezokola, the Supreme Court noted (at para 94) that the size of an organization can assist in determining the likelihood that a refugee claimant would have known of and participated in the crime or criminal purpose, and that where “the organization is multifaceted or heterogeneous, i.e. one that performs both legitimate and criminal acts, the link between the contribution and the criminal purpose will be more tenuous.”

propositions.text: RPD mentioned Habibi's testimony on duties but relied on vague evidence of police cooperation with other agencies to find complicity.
propositions.quote: Although the RPD did mention Mr. Habibi’s testimony as to his duties and activities as a police officer, it relied on vague documentary evidence which suggested that the members of the national police force “worked closely” with the Pasdaran or Komiteh and that cooperation between the Pasdaran and the police was “institutionalized” in order to find Mr. Habibi complicit in the crimes committed by other agencies of the Revolutionary regime.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD failed to address police force size and nature, relied on vague evidence to find Habibi complicit.

propositions.text: RPD's reasoning finding Habibi guilty by association is unreasonable and unjustified.
propositions.quote: This reliance, however, cannot be justified and is therefore unreasonable. The RPD in this case failed to fully assess whether Mr. Habibi had personally made a significant and knowing contribution to some crime or crime against humanity. The RPD found Mr. Habibi was associated with the national police, who were in turn associated with other enforcement agencies in Iran who committed crimes against humanity. This reasoning is inherently problematic. The RPD essentially finds Mr. Habibi guilty by association; that is, Mr. Habibi is associated with the national police force, and because the police in turn are associated with other enforcement organizations which committed crimes against humanity, that makes him complicit in those crimes.

propositions.text: No evidence showed Habibi or District 8 Police Station members participated in abuses or worked with other enforcement agencies.
propositions.quote: There was no evidence before the RPD that Mr. Habibi in particular, or other members of the District 8 Police Station in Tabriz, had participated in any abuses or played any role in working with other enforcement agencies.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD's guilty-by-association reasoning unreasonable; no evidence of Habibi's personal involvement in abuses.

propositions.text: RPD's erroneous complicity conclusion alone justifies returning matter for re-determination.
propositions.quote: The RPD’s erroneous conclusion concerning Mr. Habibi’s complicity is sufficient in itself to return the matter to the RPD for re-determination.

propositions.text: RPD's negative credibility findings on Habibi affected assessment of Applicants' fear of persecution.
propositions.quote: However, it is necessary to briefly address this final issue because the RPD’s negative credibility findings about Mr. Habibi when assessing his alleged complicity infected its assessment of each of the Applicants’ fear of persecution.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD's erroneous complicity conclusion justifies remand; negative credibility findings affected fear of persecution assessment.

propositions.text: Plausibility findings require clearest cases with clear explanation, per established jurisprudence.
propositions.quote: It is well established that plausibility findings should only be made in the clearest of cases; that is, where the facts presented are outside the realm of what could reasonably be expected or where the documentary evidence demonstrates that the events could not have happened in the manner asserted by the claimant (Valtchev v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2001 FCT 776 at paras 7, 17, 208 FTR 267), and with a clear explanation for those findings (Saeedi v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2013 FC 146 at para 30, [2013] FCJ No 173) (see also: Cortes v Canada (Citizenship and Immigration), 2014 FC 598 at para 19, 242 ACWS (3d) 167).

paragraphs.summary: The court states plausibility findings require clearest cases and clear explanation, citing established jurisprudence.

propositions.text: RPD doubted Applicants' Christian practice in Iran due to Bible study attendance in Toronto, drawing negative inference.
propositions.quote: The RPD questioned why the Applicants were required to go to Bible study sessions in Toronto if they had been practicing Christians in Iran, and because of this attendance drew a negative inference as to whether they had in fact been practising Christians in Iran.

propositions.text: This negative inference was unjustified and unreasonable as RPD ignored evidence that Bible study attendance is reasonable for converts in Iran.
propositions.quote: This inference is neither justifiable nor reasonable because the RPD ignored evidence before it in the National Documentation Package for Iran which suggests that attendance at Bible study sessions could be reasonable for someone who had converted to Christianity through an underground church in Iran because there are different levels of Christian knowledge for converts in Iran.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds RPD's negative inference on Applicants' Christian practice unreasonable, ignoring evidence on Bible study attendance.

propositions.text: Judicial review allowed; matter returned to RPD for re-determination by different panel; no question certified.
propositions.quote: For the reasons stated above, this application for judicial review is allowed and the matter is returned for re-determination by a different panel member of the RPD in accordance with these reasons. Neither party suggested a question for certification; so, no such question is certified.

paragraphs.summary: The court allows judicial review, returns matter to RPD for re-determination by different panel, and declines certification.
